Deep eutectic solvent-driven mild lignocellulose pretreatment: Unlocking lignin valorization and carbohydrate digestibility
Yang Wang a,1, Qiaoling Liu b,1, Chuanyu Yan a ID, Guoyong Song a,*, William S. Price c,* ID, Gang Zheng c ID, Allan M. Torres c, Zhimin Xue a,c,* ID

ª Beijing Key Laboratory of Lignocellulosic Chemistry, Beijing Forestry University, Beijing 100083, China ᵇ Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Anhui Agricultural University, Hefei 230036, China ᶜ Nanoscale Organisation and Dynamics Group, School of Science, Western Sydney University, Locked Bag 1797, Penrith, NSW 2751, Australia
ARTICLE INFO --- *Keywords:* Lignocellulose valorization Deep eutectic solvent Lignin extraction Native structure

ABSTRACT High-value utilization of lignocellulose and its components is generally constrained by the pretreatment effi-ciency and the structural robustness of fractionated components. Harsh pretreatment conditions can promote pretreatment efficiency but also cause serious condensation of lignin structure, thus inhibiting the depolymer-ization of lignin into valuable chemicals. Herein, we designed a novel deep eutectic solvent (DES) composed of pyridine hydrochloride, ethylene glycol, and AlCl3 for the pretreatment of lignocellulose. In the developed DES, the lignocellulose could be efficiently fractionated into the natural lignin derivatives with satisfactory hydro-genolysis reactivity and the carbohydrate fraction with high enzymatic digestibility owing to the synthesized DES having adjustable hydrogen-bond acidity, high affinity for lignin, and good protection role on lignin structure. After being pretreated under a mild fractionation condition (70°C, 6 h), a promising delignification ratio of 70.4 % was obtained for poplar, and the extracted lignin exhibited native substructure with well-preserved β-O-4 linkages (42.1 per 100 aromatic units), abundant hydroxyl groups content (4.97 mmol/g), and high molecular weight (5643 g/mol). These structural features contributed to the conversion of the obtained lignin into aromatic monomers with a high yield (27.4%). Besides, the pretreated residue could be efficiently converted into glucose with a yield of 88.2% due to the abundant hydroxyl groups of lignin in the cellulose-rich residues. Remarkably, comprehensive studies of lignin structural evolution during pretreatment revealed that the structure-controllable lignin could be effectively isolated by modulating the hydrogen-bond acidity of DESs. This work proposed a mild and efficient lignin-first biorefinery approach that was conducive to the integrated valorization of lignocellulose.

1. Introduction Utilization of lignocellulosic biomass as a renewable energy resource is a promising alternative to reduce current dependence on petro- chemical resources. Nevertheless, lignocellulose is a rigid matrix of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin intertwined through an abundance of covalent and hydrogen bonds, which complicates processing it into fuels, chemicals, and functional materials [1,2]. Fractionation of ligno- cellulose, which involves deconstruction of plant cell walls, is important for the complete and efficient utilization of these three main constituents [3]. During lignocellulose fractionation, the reaction intensity (high temperature, high pressure, high acidity) tends to be directly propor- tional to the delignification ratio and inversely proportional to the lignin

activity and cellulose retention [4]. Efficient delignification generally involves harsh pretreatment conditions, and the resulting high-purity cellulose has many applications in enzymatic saccharification and the production of cellulose nanofiber [5,6]. However, irreversible condensation under harsh environments is a commonly used procedure that severely obstructs the facile, effective, and selective transformation of lignin [7]. Thus, developing efficient delignification methods without seriously affecting the structural integrity of lignin is a critical issue in the co-valorization of carbohydrates and lignin.

In order to achieve efficient valorization of lignin and carbohydrates, lignin-first biorefinery strategies have been proposed to protectively fractionate active lignin while facilitating delignification [8–10]. These strategies include mild organosolv pretreatment [11–13], ammonia-

based pretreatment [14,15], and ionic liquid fractionation [16]. The success of these methods was attributed to the use of protective media and mild processing conditions, which allowed the extent of cleaving ẞ-aryl ether bonds and forming reactive benzylic intermediates to be diminished, thus facilitating the preservation of ẞ-O-4 linkages and decreasing the condensation ratio. Alternatively, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are promising green solvents with highly favorable properties, including low vapor pressure, non-volatile, low cost, easy preparation, and tunable properties [17–19]. Owing to the tunable properties of DESs, the structural integrity of fractionated lignin can be ensured by selecting protective reagents as DESs components [20]. For example, Barta's group showed that the introduction of ethylene glycol (EG) into the choline chloride/oxalic acid DES could protect the ẞ-O-4 linkages in birch lignin during pretreatment at 100°C for 24 h, which eventually resulted in a significant improvement in monophenol and glucose yields [21]. Xu et al. reported that pretreatment of bagasse with choline chloride/glyoxylic acid monohydrate DESs at 100°C for 9 h could pre- serve high ẞ-O-4 content (48.3/100 Ar) lignin at a delignification ratio of 68% [22]. Bian's group observed that 37.5% delignification of corncob was achieved by using ethylene glycol/oxalic acid DES at 70°C for 6 h and the regenerated lignin maintained extremely high ẞ-O-4 sub- structures (56.2/100 Ar) [23]. Despite the promising performance of DESs pretreatment in lignin extraction with structural integrity, the corresponding low delignification ratios and relatively harsh conditions (high temperature, and/or long time) were still unsatisfactory.

To achieve good co-valorization of lignin and carbohydrates, novel DESs which can promote delignification efficiency while maintaining good preservation of lignin structural integrity under mild pretreatment conditions is highly desired. As has been noted, the uneven distribution of electron density in N-heterocyclic compounds can strongly affect their interactions with electron-dense molecules [24]. Lignin is an aromatic polymer with a higher electron density than cellulose and hemicellulose, which results in lignin having a unique affinity for N-heterocyclic compounds. Lin et al. demonstrated that the pyrazole-lactic acid DES displayed a high affinity to lignin and could selectively extract lignin from wheat straw with a yield of up to 80% and a ẞ-O-4 content of up to 39/100 Ar [25]. Inspired by these results, a novel DES (denoted PEA- DESS) composed of pyridine hydrochloride (PH), EG, and AlCl3 were constructed for mild pretreatment of various lignocelluloses with the purpose of regenerating as much lignin with structural integrity as possible. We hypothesized that the acidic environment provided by AlCl3 during PEA-DESS pretreatment would effectively deconstruct lignocellulose, while PH would enhance the affinity for lignin thus accelerating lignin dissociation, and the subsequently dissociated lignin would be protected by EG through nucleophilic addition. Initially, a comprehensive study was carried out to evaluate the delignification efficiency of the novel DES on different lignocelluloses as well as the structural integrity of the extracted lignin. Subsequently, the evolution of lignin during the pretreatment process of DESs with different hydrogen-bond acidity was investigated in detail, and the possible mechanisms of fractionation and lignin protection were proposed. Finally, the specific high-value conversion of the pretreated fractions was conducted.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and reagents The lignocellulosic biomasses (poplar, pine, bagasse) used in this study were sourced from an experimental field in Beijing, China. These biomasses were processed into powders and subsequently sieved using 50-mesh nets. Before being used in the pretreatment, each lignocellulosic biomass was pre-extracted with toluene/ethanol (2:1, v/v) to remove wax. The cellulase (Cellic CTec2, 100 FPU/mL) was obtained from Novozymes Investment Co., Ltd., China. Pyridine hydrochloride (98 %) and ethylene glycol (99 %) were purchased from Macklin

Chemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China), and aluminum chloride (98%) was supplied by Aladdin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). All commercial chemicals were used directly without further purification.

## 2.2. Preparation and characterization of PEA-DESS The desired PEA-DESs were prepared by heating a mixture of PH, EG, and AlCl3 at the desired molar ratio at 70°C until a homogeneous transparent liquid was produced. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β, and π*, quantifying hydrogen-bond acidity, hydrogen-bond basicity, and dipolarity/polarizability, respectively), which can be used to characterize the chemical properties of DESs [26], were determined according to the procedure reported previously [27], and the relevant formulas are listed in the Supporting Information.

## 2.3. Lignocellulose pretreatment and lignin fractionation with PEA-DESS In a typical preparation, 3 g of lignocellulose was added to 45 g of the prepared DES in a sealed flask and heated at designated temperatures (e. g., 70, 80, and 90°C) for 6 h under continuous stirring. Then the mixture was cooled and diluted with 100 mL anhydrous ethanol, and the cellulose-rich residues were recovered by filtration (washed with extra 200 mL EtOH) and dried in a desiccator. The ethanol was evaporated from the filtrate by rotary evaporation to obtain lignin-rich DES fraction. Subsequently, the concentrated filtrate was precipitated in dilute HCl (pH = 2) and filtered to obtain lignin. The cellulolytic enzyme lignin (CEL) was extracted from lignocellulose (poplar, pine and bagasse) as described in the Supporting Information. The compositions of the raw and pretreated lignocellulose were determined according to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory standard analytical method (NREL/TP-510-42618) [28]. The delignification ratio and lignin yield were calculated as follows:
Delignification ratio = (m₁ - m₂)/m₁ × 100% (1) Lignin yield = m₃/m₁ × 100% (2)
where m₁ and m₂ were the mass of lignin in the raw lignocellulose and pretreated residue (g), respectively. m₃ was the mass of regenerated lignin.

2.4. *Enzymatic hydrolysis of reactive residues from the DESs pretreatment* In a typical preparation, the obtained residue (200 mg), sodium acetate buffer (50 mM, pH 4.8, 10 mL) and cellulase preparation (15 FPU/g) were added into a stoppered Erlenmeyer flask. Then, enzymatic hydrolysis was conducted at 50°C in an incubator shaker at 150 rpm for 72 h. During the enzymatic hydrolysis, 100 µL aliquots were taken at different incubation times and the amount of glucose generated was determined using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). The glucose yield was calculated from:
Glucose yield = $\frac{\text{glucose in the hydrolysate (g)} \times 0.9}{\text{cellulose in the solid residue (g)}} \times 100\%$ (3)

2.5. _Structural characterizations of extracted lignin_ FT-IR spectra of lignin were recorded in the wavenumber range of 4000–600 cm⁻¹ on a Bruker Tensor II spectrometer (Bruker, Germany) using the potassium bromide pellet technique.

All NMR analyses of lignin were recorded on a Bruker Avance 500 MHz spectrometer (Bruker, Germany) and the results were processed in Bruker TopSpin 4.1.3 software. For the 2D heteronuclear single-quantum coherence (HSQC) NMR analysis, 50 mg of lignin was dissolved in 0.5 mL of DMSO-d6. ## 2.6. Valorization of PEA-extracted lignin ### 2.6.1. De-etherification of PEA-extracted lignin In a typical procedure, 200 mg of extracted lignin was dissolved in 5 mL 1,4-dioxane/water (2:1, vol/vol) containing 0.1 M HCl and heated in a sealed pressure-resistant tube at 100°C for 5 h. Subsequently, the
lignin solution was added dropwise to 50 mL of deionized water to regenerate the de-etherified lignin, which was collected by filtration and freeze dried.

2.6.2. Catalytic hydrogenolysis of the PEA-extracted lignin The catalytic hydrogenolysis of lignin has been described in the literature [32]. In a representative preparation, 50 mg of the extracted lignin, 5 mL methanol and 50 mg Ru/C were placed into a 50 mL Parr autoclave (Parr Instrument Company). The reactor was sealed and purged with H2 three times to expel air, then charged with 3 MPa H2. The reaction was conducted at 200 °C with a stirring speed of 400 rpm for 12h. After the completion of the reaction, the insoluble fraction was removed by filtration, and lignin oily products were obtained from the soluble fraction by rotary evaporation. Tetradecane, as internal standard, was added to the lignin oily solution in anhydrous THF and stirred for 10 min. ### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Evaluation of delignification efficiency and lignin yields Generally, the pretreatment efficiency of poplar was closely related to the molar ratio of components in the DESs and the employed pretreatment temperature. Therefore, a detailed optimization of the reaction conditions was performed and analyzed (Fig. 1 and Table S1), including AlCl3 molar contents (0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4) and temperatures (50, 70, and 90°C). Initially, the effect of the AlCl3 molar content in DESs was investigated at 70°C. With an increase of AlCl3 content from 0 to 0.4, the hemicellulose and lignin recovery decreased from 21.1 % to 5.2 % and 24.3 % to 4.8 % (Fig. 1a), respectively, and the delignification ratio increased significantly from 30.9 % to 90.6 % (Fig. 1b). These results demonstrated that increasing AlCl3 content promoted lignocellulose fractionation. Probably, the number and strength of electrostatic/ anionic hydrogen-bond interactions between Cl⁻ with lignin increased with increasing of AlCl3 content, thus facilitating lignin removal [33]. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β and π*) were able to effectively reflect chemical properties of the DESs, and the parameters for the prepared DESs were determined and are tabulated in Table S2. As reported, DESs possessing higher α value exhibited better lignin dissociation capacity [34]. Obviously, the α value of PEA-DESs was most significantly affected by the AlCl3 content. The α value increased from 1.17 to 1.75 when the AlCl3 molar content increased linearly from 0 to 0.4 (α value = 1.43nAlCl3 + 1.2, R²: 0.97) (Fig. S1a). Remarkably, the delignification ratio showed a linear correlation (delignification ratio = 100.6α-83.9, R²: 0.97) with the α value of PEA-DESS (Fig. S1b). Therefore, the addition of AlCl3 as a Lewis acid could effectively enhance the hydrogen bonding acidity of DESs, resulting in easy donation of H-bonds to liberate H⁺, which could promote the

cleavage of the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC) linkages and β-aryl ether bonds to dissociate lignin [35,36]. Moreover, AlCl3 competed with pyridine hydrochloride for the hydroxyl groups of ethylene glycol. Thus, more and stronger anionic hydrogen bonds were formed to release the pyridine cation with unevenly distributed electron density, which could further increase the affinity of DESs to the lignin with high electron density, thereby facilitating delignification [25].

In summary, the excellent performance of PEA-DESs on low-temperature pretreatment originated from the synergistic effects of enhanced hydrogen-bond acidity by AlCl3 and the improved affinity of pyridine hydrochloride to lignin. Subsequently, the effect of temperature on pretreatment efficiency was studied using the PEA-DES with a molar ratio of 1:4:0.2 (Fig. 1c-d). The delignification ratio increased from 32.5% to 95.1% as the temperature was increased from 50 to 90°C. This was primarily because higher pretreatment temperatures enhanced the deconstruction of plant cell walls, enabling the cleavage of covalent and hydrogen bonds in LCC and lignin macromolecules by PEA-DESs. Notably, the lignin yield was lower than the delignification rate (Fig. 1b, d), which might result from the excessive depolymerization of lignin and structural functionalization during pretreatment [23].

Meanwhile, the intact syringyl-type (S-type) unit (52.1/100 Ar) and guaiacyl-type (G-type) unit (47.9/100 Ar) sig- nals were exhibited in the aromatic region of CEL (Fig. 2). In compari- son, PEA-DESs as an acidic solvent could promote the formation of benzylic intermediates via a dehydration step at the α-OH of β-O-4 substructure [11]. Therefore, the structure of lignin obtained from the PEA-DESs pretreatment was different in comparison with CEL. In particular, the addition reaction of ethylene glycol and active carboca- tion intermediates could occur in the PEA$_{0.2}$-L. Obviously, in the side- chain spectrum of PEA$_{0.2}$-L, a new cross-peak at δC/δH of 70.5/3.36 (A’$_{EG}$) which was assigned to the methylene carbons of EG clearly indicated that EG had been successfully incorporated into the lignin structure. Likewise, the Cα-Hα signal of EG-substituted β-O-4 substruc- ture was identified at δC/δH of 80.9/4.57 (A’α). Importantly, EG acted as an effective stabilization reagent for lignin functionalization, protecting the β-aryl ether bonds from cleavage and inhibiting subsequent condensation [21,37]. The α-alkoxylated β-O-4 content in PEA$_{0.2}$-L was 42.1/100 Ar, which was similar to that of CEL. However, the signal of the native β-O-4 linkage became invisible, suggesting that AlCl$_{3}$ was an effective catalyst for the dehydration of α-OH in β-O-4 motifs and the alkoxylation of ethylene glycol with lignin. Furthermore, weak condensation signals (condensed S: 5.4%) in the spectrum of PEA$_{0.2}$-L were also observed, implying that the incorporation of EG into lignin could block subsequent lignin condensation. In addition, the S/G value in PEA$_{0.2}$-L (1.44) was higher than that in CEL (1.09), and the contents of S-type units increased slightly from 52.1/100 Ar to 55.9/100 Ar while the G-type units decreased significantly from 47.9/100 Ar to 38.7/100 Ar, probably because G-type units of lignin were preferentially degraded over S-type units during PEA-DESs pretreatment. Unlike CEL, the cross- peak of p-hydroxybenzoate substructure (PB) was weakened in PEA$_{0.2}$-L,

indicating effective disruption of the ester bonds between the PB units and carbohydrate [38,39]. Based on the results above, it was deduced that PEA-DESs-assisted fractionation caused efficient lignin dissociation along with a substantial retention of β-O-4 substructures.

Characteristic functional groups on PEA-DES-extracted lignin were confirmed by FT-IR (Fig. 3a). The lignin extracted by PEA-DESS (PEA₀.₂-L) showed almost all the characteristics absorption bands compared with CEL, including distinct absorption peaks for the aromatic ring (1596, 1506, 1425 cm⁻¹), unconjugated carboxyl group (1708 cm⁻¹), hydroxyl group (3425 cm⁻¹), S-type units (1329, 1124 cm⁻¹), and G-type units (1268, 1225, 1035 cm⁻¹) [40,41], which implied that PEA₀.₂-L preserved the structure of native lignin. Nevertheless, one significant difference was observed. The stretching vibration for the conjugated carbonyl groups detected at 1658 cm⁻¹ in the CEL disappeared in the spectra of PEA₀.₂-L. As has been previously reported, the carbonyl group as an oxygen-containing polar unsaturated group readily undergoes addition reactions with oxygen-containing nucleophilic reagents (like EG) [42]. Thus, the disappearance of the carbonyl signals in the PEA₀.₂-L side chain is mainly attributed to the nucleophilic addition of EG in PEA-DESS.

Hydroxyl groups are an important functional group in lignin, which not only increases the hydrophilicity of lignin, but also facilitates various chemical reactions of lignin. The content of different types of hydroxyl groups was determined using ³¹P NMR (Fig. S2). As shown in Fig. 3b, the content of aliphatic hydroxyl groups in PEA-DESs decreased mildly compared to that in CEL, which was attributed to the conversion of hydroxyl groups to form benzylic carbocation intermediates by the dehydration and acylation in the acidic PEA-DESS [43]. Further, the change in the aliphatic OH group content was also associated with alkoxylation of the dehydrated lignin with EG. 3.5. Fractionation and structural evolution mechanism of lignin by PEA- DESs pretreatment

The mechanism for fractionation and structural evolution of lignin during the PEA-DESs pretreatment is described in Fig. 7. It was well known that lignocellulose is a remarkably complex assembly of cel- lulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [53]. During the pretreatment of lignocellulose with PEA-DESs, the added AlCl3 enhanced the hydrogen- bond acidity and assisted the release of pyridine cations. The high hydrogen-bond acidity of PEA-DESs efficiently cleaved the benzyl ester and benzyl ether bonds in LCCs as well as the β-aryl ether bonds in lignin, leading to significant removal of hemicellulose and lignin [27,35]. Furthermore, pyridine cations with uneven electron density distribution have a strong electron-withdrawing nitrogen, which can strengthen the hydrogen bonding with aromatics and phenolics, affording a higher affinity to lignin and thus facilitating dissociation [24,25]. Meanwhile, the α-OH in the β-aryl ether linkages of lignin were protonated by H⁺ and then dehydrated to form active benzyl carboca- tion, which were stabilized by EG to primarily form α-alkoxylated β-O-4 substructures and to secondarily generate a condensed structure with G- type aromatic units. It is worth noting that lignin condensation generally occurs on the active benzyl carbocation from S-type lignin. Additionally, weak depolymerization occurred during the efficient dissociation of lignin by PEA-DESs, allowing the generation of fractionated lignin with natural macromolecular structure.

### 3.6. Valorization of PEA DESs-extracted lignin The relatively high content of β-aryl ether in the PEA-DESs extracted lignin makes it an attractive raw material for producing aromatic chemicals via depolymerization. However, most of the existing depolymerization methods convert protolignin, i.e., lignin with α-OH groups in the β-O-4 linkages [12]. Lignin polyol, a typical protolignin derivative with α-alkoxylated β-O-4 structures, might have an impact on their special application. Usually, functionalization-defunctionalization is essential for functional material applications of lignin [54,55]. To make this protolignin derivative compatible with the developed valorization methods, we proposed taking advantage of the reversibility of the α-etherification to convert lignin polyol into native-like lignin. The de-etherification of PEA0.2-L extracted from the poplar, pine, and bagasse

was demonstrated by the HSQC NMR analysis (Fig. 8a-c). After de- etherification, the typical cross-peak of native β-O-4 linkage was significantly increased in the PEA0.2-L from bagasse, and even reap- peared in PEA0.2-L extracted from poplar and pine. Specifically, the β-O- 4 linkages in the PEA0.2-L extracted from poplar, pine and bagasse increased from 0, 0, 5.5/100 Ar to 21.5, 25.7, 35.7/100 Ar, respectively. In all cases, substantially reduced peaks for the α-alkoxylated β-O-4 signals (A'α, A'EG) were observed, indicating that the lignin polyol de- rivative had been successfully transformed to protolignin. However, the total β-O-4 content in all the obtained lignin samples decreased to varied degrees after the de-etherification mediated by acid.

Hydrogenolysis has been considered as an important approach to convert lignin into aromatic compounds [6,56]. All the extracted PEA$_{0.2}$-L (from different lignocellulose) and the de-etherified De-PEA$_{0.2}$-L samples exhibited well-retained β-O-4 structures, which was beneficial for achieving a high yield of aromatic compounds. The yields of various lignin-derived monomers obtained by hydrogenolysis are shown in Fig. 8d and Table S7. As reported, monomers 1, 2, 3, and 4 were generally generated through the cleavage of β-O-4 linkages in lignin [57]. 3.7. Enzymolysis of cellulose-rich residues One of the main purposes of lignocellulose pretreatment was to generate cellulose-rich residues, which could be used as the raw material to produce sugars via saccharification. In this study, the developed PEA-DESs demonstrated good ability for lignocellulose deconstruction and delignification under mild conditions, and the cellulose retention in the residues exceeded 90 %, which facilitated a high sugar yield by enzymatic saccharification. Among the cellulose-rich residues obtained from the poplar pretreatment, the residue from the PEA-DESs(1:4:0.2) pretreatment system at 70 °C provided the highest fermentable sugar yield (88.2 % glucose) after the enzymolysis of the cellulose-rich residue for 72 h. This yield was 4.6 times higher than that released from the raw poplar (Fig. S4a), which was mainly attributed to efficient removal of lignin and hemicellulose by the developed PEA-DESs, thus being beneficial for the interaction between cellulose and enzymes. However, further removal of lignin and hemicellulose reduced the glucose yield. The residue from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4) pretreatment system exhibited lower enzymatic hydrolysis activity than that from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2) pretreatment system, but a high glucose yield (81.5 %) was still achieved. The lower glucose yield from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4)-generated residue was mainly caused by the lignin structure in the generated cellulose-rich residues. It was demonstrated that the hydrophobic interaction between the lignin in cellulose-rich residue and cellulase showed a long-range attraction (the main driver for the nonproductive adsorption behavior of cellulase on lignin), especially for

the condensed lignin with stronger hydrophobicity [59]. As discussed above, more acidic PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4) caused greater lignin condensation in the cellulose-rich residue, enhancing the lignin-cellulase hydrophobic interactions, which resulted in a lower enzymatic activity than that of the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2)-generated residue. In addition, the bagasse residue obtained from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2) system gave an extremely high glucose yield of 95.6% after the same enzymatic hydrolysis (Fig. S4b). In conclusion, the EG was grafted onto the α-position of the lignin side chain to form α-etherified lignin polyol, which effectively constrained the lignin condensation and preserved hydrophilicity of the lignin side chain region, thus limiting nonproductive lignin-enzyme interactions. This was the primary reason for the high sugar yield from the cellulose-rich residues obtained in the proposed PEA-DESs pretreatment system, this holds promise for the development of economically viable and cost-effective enzyme-mediated biorefinery processes.

4. Conclusions In summary, reactive PEA-DESs were developed to fractionate lignocellulose, eventually resulting in efficient co-valorization of lignin and polysaccharide fractions. PEA-DESs were able to mildly and efficiently fractionate lignin with natural structures (well-preserved β-O-4 linkage, abundant hydroxyl groups, and high molecular weight) from lignocelluloses (poplar, pine, and bagasse) by the synergistic effect of high hydrogen-bond acidity and high lignin affinity. During the PEA-DESs pretreatment, lignin was efficiently dissociated and modified by ethylene glycol through α-alkoxylation that facilitated high retention of β-O-4 linkages and markedly blocked lignin recondensation, contributing to the high yield of aromatic monomers. In addition, hydroxyl-rich lignin decreased the nonproductive adsorption of cellulase, thus promoting the enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose-rich residues to generate

Harsh pretreatment conditions can promote pretreatment efficiency but also cause serious condensation of lignin structure, thus inhibiting the depolymer-ization of lignin into valuable chemicals. Herein, we designed a novel deep eutectic solvent (DES) composed of pyridine hydrochloride, ethylene glycol, and AlCl3 for the pretreatment of lignocellulose. In the developed DES, the lignocellulose could be efficiently fractionated into the natural lignin derivatives with satisfactory hydro-genolysis reactivity and the carbohydrate fraction with high enzymatic digestibility owing to the synthesized DES having adjustable hydrogen-bond acidity, high affinity for lignin, and good protection role on lignin structure. After being pretreated under a mild fractionation condition (70°C, 6 h), a promising delignification ratio of 70.4 % was obtained for poplar, and the extracted lignin exhibited native substructure with well-preserved β-O-4 linkages (42.1 per 100 aromatic units), abundant hydroxyl groups content (4.97 mmol/g), and high molecular weight (5643 g/mol). These structural features contributed to the conversion of the obtained lignin into aromatic monomers with a high yield (27.4%). Besides, the pretreated residue could be efficiently converted into glucose with a yield of 88.2% due to the abundant hydroxyl groups of lignin in the cellulose-rich residues. Remarkably, comprehensive studies of lignin structural evolution during pretreatment revealed that the structure-controllable lignin could be effectively isolated by modulating the hydrogen-bond acidity of DESs. This work proposed a mild and efficient lignin-first biorefinery approach that was conducive to the integrated valorization of lignocellulose. 1. Introduction Utilization of lignocellulosic biomass as a renewable energy resource is a promising alternative to reduce current dependence on petro- chemical resources. Nevertheless, lignocellulose is a rigid matrix of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin intertwined through an abundance of covalent and hydrogen bonds, which complicates processing it into fuels, chemicals, and functional materials [1,2]. Fractionation of ligno- cellulose, which involves deconstruction of plant cell walls, is important for the complete and efficient utilization of these three main constituents [3]. During lignocellulose fractionation, the reaction intensity (high temperature, high pressure, high acidity) tends to be directly propor- tional to the delignification ratio and inversely proportional to the lignin activity and cellulose retention [4]. Efficient delignification generally involves harsh pretreatment conditions, and the resulting high-purity cellulose has many applications in enzymatic saccharification and the production of cellulose nanofiber [5,6]. However, irreversible condensation under harsh environments is a commonly used procedure that severely obstructs the facile, effective, and selective transformation of lignin [7]. Thus, developing efficient delignification methods without seriously affecting the structural integrity of lignin is a critical issue in the co-valorization of carbohydrates and lignin. In order to achieve efficient valorization of lignin and carbohydrates, lignin-first biorefinery strategies have been proposed to protectively fractionate active lignin while facilitating delignification [8–10]. The success of these methods was attributed to the use of protective media and mild processing conditions, which allowed the extent of cleaving ẞ-aryl ether bonds and forming reactive benzylic intermediates to be diminished, thus facilitating the preservation of ẞ-O-4 linkages and decreasing the condensation ratio. Alternatively, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are promising green solvents with highly favorable properties, including low vapor pressure, non-volatile, low cost, easy preparation, and tunable properties [17–19]. Owing to the tunable properties of DESs, the structural integrity of fractionated lignin can be ensured by selecting protective reagents as DESs components [20]. For example, Barta's group showed that the introduction of ethylene glycol (EG) into the choline chloride/oxalic acid DES could protect the ẞ-O-4 linkages in birch lignin during pretreatment at 100°C for 24 h, which eventually resulted in a significant improvement in monophenol and glucose yields [21]. Xu et al. reported that pretreatment of bagasse with choline chloride/glyoxylic acid monohydrate DESs at 100°C for 9 h could pre- serve high ẞ-O-4 content (48.3/100 Ar) lignin at a delignification ratio of 68% [22]. Bian's group observed that 37.5% delignification of corncob was achieved by using ethylene glycol/oxalic acid DES at 70°C for 6 h and the regenerated lignin maintained extremely high ẞ-O-4 sub- structures (56.2/100 Ar) [23]. Despite the promising performance of DESs pretreatment in lignin extraction with structural integrity, the corresponding low delignification ratios and relatively harsh conditions (high temperature, and/or long time) were still unsatisfactory. To achieve good co-valorization of lignin and carbohydrates, novel DESs which can promote delignification efficiency while maintaining good preservation of lignin structural integrity under mild pretreatment conditions is highly desired. As has been noted, the uneven distribution of electron density in N-heterocyclic compounds can strongly affect their interactions with electron-dense molecules [24]. Lignin is an aromatic polymer with a higher electron density than cellulose and hemicellulose, which results in lignin having a unique affinity for N-heterocyclic compounds. Lin et al. demonstrated that the pyrazole-lactic acid DES displayed a high affinity to lignin and could selectively extract lignin from wheat straw with a yield of up to 80% and a ẞ-O-4 content of up to 39/100 Ar [25]. Inspired by these results, a novel DES (denoted PEA- DESS) composed of pyridine hydrochloride (PH), EG, and AlCl3 were constructed for mild pretreatment of various lignocelluloses with the purpose of regenerating as much lignin with structural integrity as possible. We hypothesized that the acidic environment provided by AlCl3 during PEA-DESS pretreatment would effectively deconstruct lignocellulose, while PH would enhance the affinity for lignin thus accelerating lignin dissociation, and the subsequently dissociated lignin would be protected by EG through nucleophilic addition. Initially, a comprehensive study was carried out to evaluate the delignification efficiency of the novel DES on different lignocelluloses as well as the structural integrity of the extracted lignin. Subsequently, the evolution of lignin during the pretreatment process of DESs with different hydrogen-bond acidity was investigated in detail, and the possible mechanisms of fractionation and lignin protection were proposed. Finally, the specific high-value conversion of the pretreated fractions was conducted. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and reagents The lignocellulosic biomasses (poplar, pine, bagasse) used in this study were sourced from an experimental field in Beijing, China. These biomasses were processed into powders and subsequently sieved using 50-mesh nets. Before being used in the pretreatment, each lignocellulosic biomass was pre-extracted with toluene/ethanol (2:1, v/v) to remove wax. The cellulase (Cellic CTec2, 100 FPU/mL) was obtained from Novozymes Investment Co., Ltd., China. Pyridine hydrochloride (98 %) and ethylene glycol (99 %) were purchased from Macklin Chemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China), and aluminum chloride (98%) was supplied by Aladdin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). All commercial chemicals were used directly without further purification. ## 2.2. Preparation and characterization of PEA-DESS The desired PEA-DESs were prepared by heating a mixture of PH, EG, and AlCl3 at the desired molar ratio at 70°C until a homogeneous transparent liquid was produced. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β, and π*, quantifying hydrogen-bond acidity, hydrogen-bond basicity, and dipolarity/polarizability, respectively), which can be used to characterize the chemical properties of DESs [26], were determined according to the procedure reported previously [27], and the relevant formulas are listed in the Supporting Information. ## 2.3. Lignocellulose pretreatment and lignin fractionation with PEA-DESS In a typical preparation, 3 g of lignocellulose was added to 45 g of the prepared DES in a sealed flask and heated at designated temperatures (e. g., 70, 80, and 90°C) for 6 h under continuous stirring. Then the mixture was cooled and diluted with 100 mL anhydrous ethanol, and the cellulose-rich residues were recovered by filtration (washed with extra 200 mL EtOH) and dried in a desiccator. The ethanol was evaporated from the filtrate by rotary evaporation to obtain lignin-rich DES fraction. Subsequently, the concentrated filtrate was precipitated in dilute HCl (pH = 2) and filtered to obtain lignin. The cellulolytic enzyme lignin (CEL) was extracted from lignocellulose (poplar, pine and bagasse) as described in the Supporting Information. The compositions of the raw and pretreated lignocellulose were determined according to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory standard analytical method (NREL/TP-510-42618) [28]. The delignification ratio and lignin yield were calculated as follows: Delignification ratio = (m₁ - m₂)/m₁ × 100% (1) Lignin yield = m₃/m₁ × 100% (2) where m₁ and m₂ were the mass of lignin in the raw lignocellulose and pretreated residue (g), respectively. m₃ was the mass of regenerated lignin. 2.4. *Enzymatic hydrolysis of reactive residues from the DESs pretreatment* In a typical preparation, the obtained residue (200 mg), sodium acetate buffer (50 mM, pH 4.8, 10 mL) and cellulase preparation (15 FPU/g) were added into a stoppered Erlenmeyer flask. Evaluation of delignification efficiency and lignin yields Generally, the pretreatment efficiency of poplar was closely related to the molar ratio of components in the DESs and the employed pretreatment temperature. Therefore, a detailed optimization of the reaction conditions was performed and analyzed (Fig. 1 and Table S1), including AlCl3 molar contents (0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4) and temperatures (50, 70, and 90°C). Initially, the effect of the AlCl3 molar content in DESs was investigated at 70°C. With an increase of AlCl3 content from 0 to 0.4, the hemicellulose and lignin recovery decreased from 21.1 % to 5.2 % and 24.3 % to 4.8 % (Fig. 1a), respectively, and the delignification ratio increased significantly from 30.9 % to 90.6 % (Fig. 1b). These results demonstrated that increasing AlCl3 content promoted lignocellulose fractionation. Probably, the number and strength of electrostatic/ anionic hydrogen-bond interactions between Cl⁻ with lignin increased with increasing of AlCl3 content, thus facilitating lignin removal [33]. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β and π*) were able to effectively reflect chemical properties of the DESs, and the parameters for the prepared DESs were determined and are tabulated in Table S2. As reported, DESs possessing higher α value exhibited better lignin dissociation capacity [34]. Obviously, the α value of PEA-DESs was most significantly affected by the AlCl3 content. The α value increased from 1.17 to 1.75 when the AlCl3 molar content increased linearly from 0 to 0.4 (α value = 1.43nAlCl3 + 1.2, R²: 0.97) (Fig. S1a). Remarkably, the delignification ratio showed a linear correlation (delignification ratio = 100.6α-83.9, R²: 0.97) with the α value of PEA-DESS (Fig. S1b). Therefore, the addition of AlCl3 as a Lewis acid could effectively enhance the hydrogen bonding acidity of DESs, resulting in easy donation of H-bonds to liberate H⁺, which could promote the cleavage of the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC) linkages and β-aryl ether bonds to dissociate lignin [35,36]. Moreover, AlCl3 competed with pyridine hydrochloride for the hydroxyl groups of ethylene glycol. Thus, more and stronger anionic hydrogen bonds were formed to release the pyridine cation with unevenly distributed electron density, which could further increase the affinity of DESs to the lignin with high electron density, thereby facilitating delignification [25]. In summary, the excellent performance of PEA-DESs on low-temperature pretreatment originated from the synergistic effects of enhanced hydrogen-bond acidity by AlCl3 and the improved affinity of pyridine hydrochloride to lignin. Subsequently, the effect of temperature on pretreatment efficiency was studied using the PEA-DES with a molar ratio of 1:4:0.2 (Fig. 1c-d). The delignification ratio increased from 32.5% to 95.1% as the temperature was increased from 50 to 90°C. This was primarily because higher pretreatment temperatures enhanced the deconstruction of plant cell walls, enabling the cleavage of covalent and hydrogen bonds in LCC and lignin macromolecules by PEA-DESs. Notably, the lignin yield was lower than the delignification rate (Fig. 1b, d), which might result from the excessive depolymerization of lignin and structural functionalization during pretreatment [23]. 3.2. The lignin extracted by PEA-DESS (PEA₀.₂-L) showed almost all the characteristics absorption bands compared with CEL, including distinct absorption peaks for the aromatic ring (1596, 1506, 1425 cm⁻¹), unconjugated carboxyl group (1708 cm⁻¹), hydroxyl group (3425 cm⁻¹), S-type units (1329, 1124 cm⁻¹), and G-type units (1268, 1225, 1035 cm⁻¹) [40,41], which implied that PEA₀.₂-L preserved the structure of native lignin. Fractionation and structural evolution mechanism of lignin by PEA- DESs pretreatment The mechanism for fractionation and structural evolution of lignin during the PEA-DESs pretreatment is described in Fig. 7. It was well known that lignocellulose is a remarkably complex assembly of cel- lulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [53]. During the pretreatment of lignocellulose with PEA-DESs, the added AlCl3 enhanced the hydrogen- bond acidity and assisted the release of pyridine cations. The high hydrogen-bond acidity of PEA-DESs efficiently cleaved the benzyl ester and benzyl ether bonds in LCCs as well as the β-aryl ether bonds in lignin, leading to significant removal of hemicellulose and lignin [27,35]. Furthermore, pyridine cations with uneven electron density distribution have a strong electron-withdrawing nitrogen, which can strengthen the hydrogen bonding with aromatics and phenolics, affording a higher affinity to lignin and thus facilitating dissociation [24,25]. Meanwhile, the α-OH in the β-aryl ether linkages of lignin were protonated by H⁺ and then dehydrated to form active benzyl carboca- tion, which were stabilized by EG to primarily form α-alkoxylated β-O-4 substructures and to secondarily generate a condensed structure with G- type aromatic units. It is worth noting that lignin condensation generally occurs on the active benzyl carbocation from S-type lignin. Additionally, weak depolymerization occurred during the efficient dissociation of lignin by PEA-DESs, allowing the generation of fractionated lignin with natural macromolecular structure. ### 3.6. Valorization of PEA DESs-extracted lignin The relatively high content of β-aryl ether in the PEA-DESs extracted lignin makes it an attractive raw material for producing aromatic chemicals via depolymerization. However, most of the existing depolymerization methods convert protolignin, i.e., lignin with α-OH groups in the β-O-4 linkages [12]. Lignin polyol, a typical protolignin derivative with α-alkoxylated β-O-4 structures, might have an impact on their special application. Usually, functionalization-defunctionalization is essential for functional material applications of lignin [54,55]. To make this protolignin derivative compatible with the developed valorization methods, we proposed taking advantage of the reversibility of the α-etherification to convert lignin polyol into native-like lignin. The de-etherification of PEA0.2-L extracted from the poplar, pine, and bagasse was demonstrated by the HSQC NMR analysis (Fig. 8a-c). After de- etherification, the typical cross-peak of native β-O-4 linkage was significantly increased in the PEA0.2-L from bagasse, and even reap- peared in PEA0.2-L extracted from poplar and pine. Specifically, the β-O- 4 linkages in the PEA0.2-L extracted from poplar, pine and bagasse increased from 0, 0, 5.5/100 Ar to 21.5, 25.7, 35.7/100 Ar, respectively. In all cases, substantially reduced peaks for the α-alkoxylated β-O-4 signals (A'α, A'EG) were observed, indicating that the lignin polyol de- rivative had been successfully transformed to protolignin. However, the total β-O-4 content in all the obtained lignin samples decreased to varied degrees after the de-etherification mediated by acid. Hydrogenolysis has been considered as an important approach to convert lignin into aromatic compounds [6,56]. All the extracted PEA$_{0.2}$-L (from different lignocellulose) and the de-etherified De-PEA$_{0.2}$-L samples exhibited well-retained β-O-4 structures, which was beneficial for achieving a high yield of aromatic compounds. The yields of various lignin-derived monomers obtained by hydrogenolysis are shown in Fig. 8d and Table S7. As reported, monomers 1, 2, 3, and 4 were generally generated through the cleavage of β-O-4 linkages in lignin [57]. Because the contents of total β-O-4 linkages in CEL, PEA$_{0.2}$-L, and De-PEA$_{0.2}$-L from poplar and pine decreased, the yield of the targeted monomers decreased gradually, suggesting that the β-O-4 linkage content was the crucial factor affecting the yield of monophenols. In particular, the monomer yield from PEA$_{0.2}$-L-poplar with a β-O-4 linkage of 42.1/100 Ar was 27.5 %, which is roughly 7 times higher than that reported for other acidic DESs-extracted lignin [21]. Moreover, it was observed that the yields of monophenols from various PEA$_{0.2}$-L samples were only slightly lower than those from the corresponding CEL samples (Fig. 8d) because of the lower contents of β-O-4 linkages in PEA$_{0.2}$-L than that in CEL. Nevertheless, the product distribution was relatively uniform in both CEL and PEA$_{0.2}$-L, suggesting that PEA-DESs extracted lignin with well-preserved β-aryl ether bonds is a very promising alternative to protolignin. Enzymolysis of cellulose-rich residues One of the main purposes of lignocellulose pretreatment was to generate cellulose-rich residues, which could be used as the raw material to produce sugars via saccharification. In this study, the developed PEA-DESs demonstrated good ability for lignocellulose deconstruction and delignification under mild conditions, and the cellulose retention in the residues exceeded 90 %, which facilitated a high sugar yield by enzymatic saccharification. Among the cellulose-rich residues obtained from the poplar pretreatment, the residue from the PEA-DESs(1:4:0.2) pretreatment system at 70 °C provided the highest fermentable sugar yield (88.2 % glucose) after the enzymolysis of the cellulose-rich residue for 72 h. This yield was 4.6 times higher than that released from the raw poplar (Fig. S4a), which was mainly attributed to efficient removal of lignin and hemicellulose by the developed PEA-DESs, thus being beneficial for the interaction between cellulose and enzymes. However, further removal of lignin and hemicellulose reduced the glucose yield. The residue from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4) pretreatment system exhibited lower enzymatic hydrolysis activity than that from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2) pretreatment system, but a high glucose yield (81.5 %) was still achieved. The lower glucose yield from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4)-generated residue was mainly caused by the lignin structure in the generated cellulose-rich residues. It was demonstrated that the hydrophobic interaction between the lignin in cellulose-rich residue and cellulase showed a long-range attraction (the main driver for the nonproductive adsorption behavior of cellulase on lignin), especially for the condensed lignin with stronger hydrophobicity [59]. As discussed above, more acidic PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4) caused greater lignin condensation in the cellulose-rich residue, enhancing the lignin-cellulase hydrophobic interactions, which resulted in a lower enzymatic activity than that of the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2)-generated residue. In addition, the bagasse residue obtained from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2) system gave an extremely high glucose yield of 95.6% after the same enzymatic hydrolysis (Fig. S4b). In conclusion, the EG was grafted onto the α-position of the lignin side chain to form α-etherified lignin polyol, which effectively constrained the lignin condensation and preserved hydrophilicity of the lignin side chain region, thus limiting nonproductive lignin-enzyme interactions. This was the primary reason for the high sugar yield from the cellulose-rich residues obtained in the proposed PEA-DESs pretreatment system, this holds promise for the development of economically viable and cost-effective enzyme-mediated biorefinery processes. 4. Conclusions In summary, reactive PEA-DESs were developed to fractionate lignocellulose, eventually resulting in efficient co-valorization of lignin and polysaccharide fractions. PEA-DESs were able to mildly and efficiently fractionate lignin with natural structures (well-preserved β-O-4 linkage, abundant hydroxyl groups, and high molecular weight) from lignocelluloses (poplar, pine, and bagasse) by the synergistic effect of high hydrogen-bond acidity and high lignin affinity. During the PEA-DESs pretreatment, lignin was efficiently dissociated and modified by ethylene glycol through α-alkoxylation that facilitated high retention of β-O-4 linkages and markedly blocked lignin recondensation, contributing to the high yield of aromatic monomers. In addition, hydroxyl-rich lignin decreased the nonproductive adsorption of cellulase, thus promoting the enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose-rich residues to generate 10 Y. Wang et al. Notably, the evolution of lignin structure under PEA-DESs pretreatment was comprehensively investigated, which pro- vided a basis for understanding lignin dissociation and obtaining lignin with a controlled structure. Harsh pretreatment conditions can promote pretreatment efficiency but also cause serious condensation of lignin structure, thus inhibiting the depolymer-ization of lignin into valuable chemicals. Herein, we designed a novel deep eutectic solvent (DES) composed of pyridine hydrochloride, ethylene glycol, and AlCl3 for the pretreatment of lignocellulose. In the developed DES, the lignocellulose could be efficiently fractionated into the natural lignin derivatives with satisfactory hydro-genolysis reactivity and the carbohydrate fraction with high enzymatic digestibility owing to the synthesized DES having adjustable hydrogen-bond acidity, high affinity for lignin, and good protection role on lignin structure. After being pretreated under a mild fractionation condition (70°C, 6 h), a promising delignification ratio of 70.4 % was obtained for poplar, and the extracted lignin exhibited native substructure with well-preserved β-O-4 linkages (42.1 per 100 aromatic units), abundant hydroxyl groups content (4.97 mmol/g), and high molecular weight (5643 g/mol). These structural features contributed to the conversion of the obtained lignin into aromatic monomers with a high yield (27.4%). Besides, the pretreated residue could be efficiently converted into glucose with a yield of 88.2% due to the abundant hydroxyl groups of lignin in the cellulose-rich residues. Remarkably, comprehensive studies of lignin structural evolution during pretreatment revealed that the structure-controllable lignin could be effectively isolated by modulating the hydrogen-bond acidity of DESs. This work proposed a mild and efficient lignin-first biorefinery approach that was conducive to the integrated valorization of lignocellulose. 1. Introduction Utilization of lignocellulosic biomass as a renewable energy resource is a promising alternative to reduce current dependence on petro- chemical resources. Nevertheless, lignocellulose is a rigid matrix of cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin intertwined through an abundance of covalent and hydrogen bonds, which complicates processing it into fuels, chemicals, and functional materials [1,2]. Fractionation of ligno- cellulose, which involves deconstruction of plant cell walls, is important for the complete and efficient utilization of these three main constituents [3]. During lignocellulose fractionation, the reaction intensity (high temperature, high pressure, high acidity) tends to be directly propor- tional to the delignification ratio and inversely proportional to the lignin activity and cellulose retention [4]. Efficient delignification generally involves harsh pretreatment conditions, and the resulting high-purity cellulose has many applications in enzymatic saccharification and the production of cellulose nanofiber [5,6]. However, irreversible condensation under harsh environments is a commonly used procedure that severely obstructs the facile, effective, and selective transformation of lignin [7]. Thus, developing efficient delignification methods without seriously affecting the structural integrity of lignin is a critical issue in the co-valorization of carbohydrates and lignin. In order to achieve efficient valorization of lignin and carbohydrates, lignin-first biorefinery strategies have been proposed to protectively fractionate active lignin while facilitating delignification [8–10]. The success of these methods was attributed to the use of protective media and mild processing conditions, which allowed the extent of cleaving ẞ-aryl ether bonds and forming reactive benzylic intermediates to be diminished, thus facilitating the preservation of ẞ-O-4 linkages and decreasing the condensation ratio. Alternatively, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are promising green solvents with highly favorable properties, including low vapor pressure, non-volatile, low cost, easy preparation, and tunable properties [17–19]. Owing to the tunable properties of DESs, the structural integrity of fractionated lignin can be ensured by selecting protective reagents as DESs components [20]. For example, Barta's group showed that the introduction of ethylene glycol (EG) into the choline chloride/oxalic acid DES could protect the ẞ-O-4 linkages in birch lignin during pretreatment at 100°C for 24 h, which eventually resulted in a significant improvement in monophenol and glucose yields [21]. Xu et al. reported that pretreatment of bagasse with choline chloride/glyoxylic acid monohydrate DESs at 100°C for 9 h could pre- serve high ẞ-O-4 content (48.3/100 Ar) lignin at a delignification ratio of 68% [22]. Bian's group observed that 37.5% delignification of corncob was achieved by using ethylene glycol/oxalic acid DES at 70°C for 6 h and the regenerated lignin maintained extremely high ẞ-O-4 sub- structures (56.2/100 Ar) [23]. Despite the promising performance of DESs pretreatment in lignin extraction with structural integrity, the corresponding low delignification ratios and relatively harsh conditions (high temperature, and/or long time) were still unsatisfactory. To achieve good co-valorization of lignin and carbohydrates, novel DESs which can promote delignification efficiency while maintaining good preservation of lignin structural integrity under mild pretreatment conditions is highly desired. As has been noted, the uneven distribution of electron density in N-heterocyclic compounds can strongly affect their interactions with electron-dense molecules [24]. Lignin is an aromatic polymer with a higher electron density than cellulose and hemicellulose, which results in lignin having a unique affinity for N-heterocyclic compounds. Lin et al. demonstrated that the pyrazole-lactic acid DES displayed a high affinity to lignin and could selectively extract lignin from wheat straw with a yield of up to 80% and a ẞ-O-4 content of up to 39/100 Ar [25]. Inspired by these results, a novel DES (denoted PEA- DESS) composed of pyridine hydrochloride (PH), EG, and AlCl3 were constructed for mild pretreatment of various lignocelluloses with the purpose of regenerating as much lignin with structural integrity as possible. We hypothesized that the acidic environment provided by AlCl3 during PEA-DESS pretreatment would effectively deconstruct lignocellulose, while PH would enhance the affinity for lignin thus accelerating lignin dissociation, and the subsequently dissociated lignin would be protected by EG through nucleophilic addition. Initially, a comprehensive study was carried out to evaluate the delignification efficiency of the novel DES on different lignocelluloses as well as the structural integrity of the extracted lignin. Subsequently, the evolution of lignin during the pretreatment process of DESs with different hydrogen-bond acidity was investigated in detail, and the possible mechanisms of fractionation and lignin protection were proposed. Finally, the specific high-value conversion of the pretreated fractions was conducted. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and reagents The lignocellulosic biomasses (poplar, pine, bagasse) used in this study were sourced from an experimental field in Beijing, China. These biomasses were processed into powders and subsequently sieved using 50-mesh nets. Before being used in the pretreatment, each lignocellulosic biomass was pre-extracted with toluene/ethanol (2:1, v/v) to remove wax. The cellulase (Cellic CTec2, 100 FPU/mL) was obtained from Novozymes Investment Co., Ltd., China. Pyridine hydrochloride (98 %) and ethylene glycol (99 %) were purchased from Macklin Chemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China), and aluminum chloride (98%) was supplied by Aladdin Biochemical Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). All commercial chemicals were used directly without further purification. ## 2.2. Preparation and characterization of PEA-DESS The desired PEA-DESs were prepared by heating a mixture of PH, EG, and AlCl3 at the desired molar ratio at 70°C until a homogeneous transparent liquid was produced. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β, and π*, quantifying hydrogen-bond acidity, hydrogen-bond basicity, and dipolarity/polarizability, respectively), which can be used to characterize the chemical properties of DESs [26], were determined according to the procedure reported previously [27], and the relevant formulas are listed in the Supporting Information. ## 2.3. Lignocellulose pretreatment and lignin fractionation with PEA-DESS In a typical preparation, 3 g of lignocellulose was added to 45 g of the prepared DES in a sealed flask and heated at designated temperatures (e. g., 70, 80, and 90°C) for 6 h under continuous stirring. Then the mixture was cooled and diluted with 100 mL anhydrous ethanol, and the cellulose-rich residues were recovered by filtration (washed with extra 200 mL EtOH) and dried in a desiccator. The ethanol was evaporated from the filtrate by rotary evaporation to obtain lignin-rich DES fraction. Subsequently, the concentrated filtrate was precipitated in dilute HCl (pH = 2) and filtered to obtain lignin. The cellulolytic enzyme lignin (CEL) was extracted from lignocellulose (poplar, pine and bagasse) as described in the Supporting Information. The compositions of the raw and pretreated lignocellulose were determined according to the National Renewable Energy Laboratory standard analytical method (NREL/TP-510-42618) [28]. Evaluation of delignification efficiency and lignin yields Generally, the pretreatment efficiency of poplar was closely related to the molar ratio of components in the DESs and the employed pretreatment temperature. Therefore, a detailed optimization of the reaction conditions was performed and analyzed (Fig. 1 and Table S1), including AlCl3 molar contents (0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4) and temperatures (50, 70, and 90°C). Initially, the effect of the AlCl3 molar content in DESs was investigated at 70°C. With an increase of AlCl3 content from 0 to 0.4, the hemicellulose and lignin recovery decreased from 21.1 % to 5.2 % and 24.3 % to 4.8 % (Fig. 1a), respectively, and the delignification ratio increased significantly from 30.9 % to 90.6 % (Fig. 1b). These results demonstrated that increasing AlCl3 content promoted lignocellulose fractionation. Probably, the number and strength of electrostatic/ anionic hydrogen-bond interactions between Cl⁻ with lignin increased with increasing of AlCl3 content, thus facilitating lignin removal [33]. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters (α, β and π*) were able to effectively reflect chemical properties of the DESs, and the parameters for the prepared DESs were determined and are tabulated in Table S2. As reported, DESs possessing higher α value exhibited better lignin dissociation capacity [34]. Obviously, the α value of PEA-DESs was most significantly affected by the AlCl3 content. The α value increased from 1.17 to 1.75 when the AlCl3 molar content increased linearly from 0 to 0.4 (α value = 1.43nAlCl3 + 1.2, R²: 0.97) (Fig. S1a). Remarkably, the delignification ratio showed a linear correlation (delignification ratio = 100.6α-83.9, R²: 0.97) with the α value of PEA-DESS (Fig. S1b). Therefore, the addition of AlCl3 as a Lewis acid could effectively enhance the hydrogen bonding acidity of DESs, resulting in easy donation of H-bonds to liberate H⁺, which could promote the cleavage of the lignin-carbohydrate complex (LCC) linkages and β-aryl ether bonds to dissociate lignin [35,36]. Moreover, AlCl3 competed with pyridine hydrochloride for the hydroxyl groups of ethylene glycol. Thus, more and stronger anionic hydrogen bonds were formed to release the pyridine cation with unevenly distributed electron density, which could further increase the affinity of DESs to the lignin with high electron density, thereby facilitating delignification [25]. In summary, the excellent performance of PEA-DESs on low-temperature pretreatment originated from the synergistic effects of enhanced hydrogen-bond acidity by AlCl3 and the improved affinity of pyridine hydrochloride to lignin. Subsequently, the effect of temperature on pretreatment efficiency was studied using the PEA-DES with a molar ratio of 1:4:0.2 (Fig. 1c-d). The delignification ratio increased from 32.5% to 95.1% as the temperature was increased from 50 to 90°C. This was primarily because higher pretreatment temperatures enhanced the deconstruction of plant cell walls, enabling the cleavage of covalent and hydrogen bonds in LCC and lignin macromolecules by PEA-DESs. Notably, the lignin yield was lower than the delignification rate (Fig. 1b, d), which might result from the excessive depolymerization of lignin and structural functionalization during pretreatment [23]. 3.2. However, the signal of the native β-O-4 linkage became invisible, suggesting that AlCl$_{3}$ was an effective catalyst for the dehydration of α-OH in β-O-4 motifs and the alkoxylation of ethylene glycol with lignin. Furthermore, weak condensation signals (condensed S: 5.4%) in the spectrum of PEA$_{0.2}$-L were also observed, implying that the incorporation of EG into lignin could block subsequent lignin condensation. The lignin extracted by PEA-DESS (PEA₀.₂-L) showed almost all the characteristics absorption bands compared with CEL, including distinct absorption peaks for the aromatic ring (1596, 1506, 1425 cm⁻¹), unconjugated carboxyl group (1708 cm⁻¹), hydroxyl group (3425 cm⁻¹), S-type units (1329, 1124 cm⁻¹), and G-type units (1268, 1225, 1035 cm⁻¹) [40,41], which implied that PEA₀.₂-L preserved the structure of native lignin. Nevertheless, one significant difference was observed. The stretching vibration for the conjugated carbonyl groups detected at 1658 cm⁻¹ in the CEL disappeared in the spectra of PEA₀.₂-L. As has been previously reported, the carbonyl group as an oxygen-containing polar unsaturated group readily undergoes addition reactions with oxygen-containing nucleophilic reagents (like EG) [42]. Thus, the disappearance of the carbonyl signals in the PEA₀.₂-L side chain is mainly attributed to the nucleophilic addition of EG in PEA-DESS. The content of different types of hydroxyl groups was determined using ³¹P NMR (Fig. S2). Fractionation and structural evolution mechanism of lignin by PEA- DESs pretreatment The mechanism for fractionation and structural evolution of lignin during the PEA-DESs pretreatment is described in Fig. 7. It was well known that lignocellulose is a remarkably complex assembly of cel- lulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [53]. During the pretreatment of lignocellulose with PEA-DESs, the added AlCl3 enhanced the hydrogen- bond acidity and assisted the release of pyridine cations. The high hydrogen-bond acidity of PEA-DESs efficiently cleaved the benzyl ester and benzyl ether bonds in LCCs as well as the β-aryl ether bonds in lignin, leading to significant removal of hemicellulose and lignin [27,35]. Furthermore, pyridine cations with uneven electron density distribution have a strong electron-withdrawing nitrogen, which can strengthen the hydrogen bonding with aromatics and phenolics, affording a higher affinity to lignin and thus facilitating dissociation [24,25]. Meanwhile, the α-OH in the β-aryl ether linkages of lignin were protonated by H⁺ and then dehydrated to form active benzyl carboca- tion, which were stabilized by EG to primarily form α-alkoxylated β-O-4 substructures and to secondarily generate a condensed structure with G- type aromatic units. It is worth noting that lignin condensation generally occurs on the active benzyl carbocation from S-type lignin. Additionally, weak depolymerization occurred during the efficient dissociation of lignin by PEA-DESs, allowing the generation of fractionated lignin with natural macromolecular structure. ### 3.6. Valorization of PEA DESs-extracted lignin The relatively high content of β-aryl ether in the PEA-DESs extracted lignin makes it an attractive raw material for producing aromatic chemicals via depolymerization. However, most of the existing depolymerization methods convert protolignin, i.e., lignin with α-OH groups in the β-O-4 linkages [12]. Lignin polyol, a typical protolignin derivative with α-alkoxylated β-O-4 structures, might have an impact on their special application. Usually, functionalization-defunctionalization is essential for functional material applications of lignin [54,55]. To make this protolignin derivative compatible with the developed valorization methods, we proposed taking advantage of the reversibility of the α-etherification to convert lignin polyol into native-like lignin. The de-etherification of PEA0.2-L extracted from the poplar, pine, and bagasse was demonstrated by the HSQC NMR analysis (Fig. 8a-c). After de- etherification, the typical cross-peak of native β-O-4 linkage was significantly increased in the PEA0.2-L from bagasse, and even reap- peared in PEA0.2-L extracted from poplar and pine. Specifically, the β-O- 4 linkages in the PEA0.2-L extracted from poplar, pine and bagasse increased from 0, 0, 5.5/100 Ar to 21.5, 25.7, 35.7/100 Ar, respectively. In all cases, substantially reduced peaks for the α-alkoxylated β-O-4 signals (A'α, A'EG) were observed, indicating that the lignin polyol de- rivative had been successfully transformed to protolignin. However, the total β-O-4 content in all the obtained lignin samples decreased to varied degrees after the de-etherification mediated by acid. Hydrogenolysis has been considered as an important approach to convert lignin into aromatic compounds [6,56]. All the extracted PEA$_{0.2}$-L (from different lignocellulose) and the de-etherified De-PEA$_{0.2}$-L samples exhibited well-retained β-O-4 structures, which was beneficial for achieving a high yield of aromatic compounds. The yields of various lignin-derived monomers obtained by hydrogenolysis are shown in Fig. 8d and Table S7. As reported, monomers 1, 2, 3, and 4 were generally generated through the cleavage of β-O-4 linkages in lignin [57]. Because the contents of total β-O-4 linkages in CEL, PEA$_{0.2}$-L, and De-PEA$_{0.2}$-L from poplar and pine decreased, the yield of the targeted monomers decreased gradually, suggesting that the β-O-4 linkage content was the crucial factor affecting the yield of monophenols. In particular, the monomer yield from PEA$_{0.2}$-L-poplar with a β-O-4 linkage of 42.1/100 Ar was 27.5 %, which is roughly 7 times higher than that reported for other acidic DESs-extracted lignin [21]. Moreover, it was observed that the yields of monophenols from various PEA$_{0.2}$-L samples were only slightly lower than those from the corresponding CEL samples (Fig. 8d) because of the lower contents of β-O-4 linkages in PEA$_{0.2}$-L than that in CEL. Nevertheless, the product distribution was relatively uniform in both CEL and PEA$_{0.2}$-L, suggesting that PEA-DESs extracted lignin with well-preserved β-aryl ether bonds is a very promising alternative to protolignin. Enzymolysis of cellulose-rich residues One of the main purposes of lignocellulose pretreatment was to generate cellulose-rich residues, which could be used as the raw material to produce sugars via saccharification. In this study, the developed PEA-DESs demonstrated good ability for lignocellulose deconstruction and delignification under mild conditions, and the cellulose retention in the residues exceeded 90 %, which facilitated a high sugar yield by enzymatic saccharification. Among the cellulose-rich residues obtained from the poplar pretreatment, the residue from the PEA-DESs(1:4:0.2) pretreatment system at 70 °C provided the highest fermentable sugar yield (88.2 % glucose) after the enzymolysis of the cellulose-rich residue for 72 h. This yield was 4.6 times higher than that released from the raw poplar (Fig. S4a), which was mainly attributed to efficient removal of lignin and hemicellulose by the developed PEA-DESs, thus being beneficial for the interaction between cellulose and enzymes. However, further removal of lignin and hemicellulose reduced the glucose yield. The residue from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4) pretreatment system exhibited lower enzymatic hydrolysis activity than that from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2) pretreatment system, but a high glucose yield (81.5 %) was still achieved. The lower glucose yield from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4)-generated residue was mainly caused by the lignin structure in the generated cellulose-rich residues. It was demonstrated that the hydrophobic interaction between the lignin in cellulose-rich residue and cellulase showed a long-range attraction (the main driver for the nonproductive adsorption behavior of cellulase on lignin), especially for the condensed lignin with stronger hydrophobicity [59]. As discussed above, more acidic PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.4) caused greater lignin condensation in the cellulose-rich residue, enhancing the lignin-cellulase hydrophobic interactions, which resulted in a lower enzymatic activity than that of the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2)-generated residue. In addition, the bagasse residue obtained from the PEA-DESs-(1:4:0.2) system gave an extremely high glucose yield of 95.6% after the same enzymatic hydrolysis (Fig. S4b). In conclusion, the EG was grafted onto the α-position of the lignin side chain to form α-etherified lignin polyol, which effectively constrained the lignin condensation and preserved hydrophilicity of the lignin side chain region, thus limiting nonproductive lignin-enzyme interactions. This was the primary reason for the high sugar yield from the cellulose-rich residues obtained in the proposed PEA-DESs pretreatment system, this holds promise for the development of economically viable and cost-effective enzyme-mediated biorefinery processes. 4. Conclusions In summary, reactive PEA-DESs were developed to fractionate lignocellulose, eventually resulting in efficient co-valorization of lignin and polysaccharide fractions. PEA-DESs were able to mildly and efficiently fractionate lignin with natural structures (well-preserved β-O-4 linkage, abundant hydroxyl groups, and high molecular weight) from lignocelluloses (poplar, pine, and bagasse) by the synergistic effect of high hydrogen-bond acidity and high lignin affinity. During the PEA-DESs pretreatment, lignin was efficiently dissociated and modified by ethylene glycol through α-alkoxylation that facilitated high retention of β-O-4 linkages and markedly blocked lignin recondensation, contributing to the high yield of aromatic monomers. In addition, hydroxyl-rich lignin decreased the nonproductive adsorption of cellulase, thus promoting the enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose-rich residues to generate 10 Y. Wang et al. Notably, the evolution of lignin structure under PEA-DESs pretreatment was comprehensively investigated, which pro- vided a basis for understanding lignin dissociation and obtaining lignin with a controlled structure.
